title: Yoo-Hoo, Mrs. Goldberg
full_review:
Though her work has largely faded from public awareness, media pioneer Gertrude Berg (1898-1966), the creator, principal writer and leading lady of the long-running Jewish domestic comedy "The Goldbergs," was one of the most popular entertainers of radio's golden age and one of television's earliest stars.

Berg's life and superlatives-studded career are celebrated in filmmaker Aviva Kempner's warmhearted documentary "Yoo-Hoo, Mrs. Goldberg" (International Film Circuit).

Berg's brainchild, originally called "The Rise of the Goldbergs," first hit the NBC radio airwaves in 1929. At a time when ethnic groups were often mocked or caricatured, Berg's program, on which she played endearing matriarch Molly Goldberg, brought a realistic and respectful, if gently comic portrayal of New York immigrant life to the American heartland.

The series followed the day-to-day ups and downs of the middle-class clan, who lived in a tenement in the Bronx, and Molly's well-meaning efforts to solve their problems as well as those of all her neighbors. Leaning out her window to kibitz with these ladies across an airshaft, Molly would call out, "Yoo-hoo, is anybody ...? " And the greeting became a national catchphrase.

As America sank further into the Depression, Berg's scripts boosted national morale by promoting familial relationships and humane values over possessions. Berg courageously battled both Nazism and widespread domestic anti-Semitism, and helped raise millions in war bonds during World War II.

After "The Goldbergs" ended its run on radio in 1945, Berg parlayed the success of her 1948 Broadway show "Me and Molly" into a shot at television. Despite the TV version's popularity, and Berg's success as the winner of the first Emmy for best actress, the program ran afoul of the anti-communism campaign of the 1950s which succeeded in driving it off the air temporarily.

Kempner's accomplished profile uses archival footage and interviews with associates to delineate the similarities and differences between Berg and her alter ego. Though much of "The Goldbergs" was based on Berg's own family -- she was born Gertrude Edelstein and raised, in part, at her father's hotel in the Catskills -- Berg was better educated and more driven than Molly.

As excerpts from an interview with Edward R. Murrow on his series "Person to Person" also show, Berg dressed elegantly, took pride in her antiques and spoke without a trace of Molly's Yiddish accent.

Though they're only dealt with in passing, prominent Catholics of the era come off less than favorably. "Radio priest" Father Charles Coughlin, whose deplorable anti-Semitic diatribes in the 1930s eventually drew Vatican intervention, is mentioned as an embodiment of anti-Jewish sentiment.

And the screenwriter of a film based on Berg's life relates the barely credible anecdote that New York's Cardinal Francis Spellman agreed to help clear Berg of charges of communism, provided she agreed to convert to Catholicism.

The film contains mature themes, including suicide, and incidental but negative treatment of Catholic historical figures. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. Not rated by the Motion Picture Association of America.
